4Q25/1Q26: NII recovery supports growth, while fees and AQ drive divergence; downgrade BoSH and BoBJ

1Q26 results for China regional banks (CRBs) showed a continued recovery in core earnings, supported by stronger NII growth (+16% y/y for JPM-covered CRBs) and early signs of NIM stabilization. PPOP growth improved to 13% y/y in 1Q, with improvements in opex control, while bottom-line growth (+7% y/y) was capped by higher credit costs. We believe the sector is entering a more stock-specific phase, where banks with stronger core earnings recoveries and better risk control should outperform. Our top picks are BoNB and CRCB. We downgrade BoBJ to UW from Neutral and BoSH to Neutral from OW.

\- 1Q26 key trends: Broad-based NII recovery, divergent performance in fees and credit costs. CRBs delivered improvements in 1Q26 operating trends, driven mainly by stronger NII and early NIM stabilization. However, this is not yet a clean profit recovery, as fee trends remain uneven, non-fees remain volatile, and rising credit costs offset part of the PPOP improvement. CRBs' average loan growth (5% q/q in 1Q) remains stronger than SOE banks' and system levels, with corporate lending the key driver. AQ indicators remain broadly stable, but retail and SME-related risks remain the key points to watch. The CET1 buffer weakens, which could be a threat that limits asset expansion and dividend stability, as CRBs are short of external capital raising channels.

\- Top picks: BoNB and CRCB. BoNB remains our top pick among CRBs, supported by the cleanest 1Q26 beat and the most visible fee upside. We believe the combination of NII recovery, fee acceleration, improving forward-looking AQ indicators and a positive FY25 dividend surprise should continue to support BoNB's valuation premium. We also like CRCB for its improving earnings trend, the scarcity value of an ROE recovery among A-share banks, and regional advantage in the Chengdu-Chongqing economic circle. We believe CRCB's valuation of a 0.54x 2026E P/B does not fully capture the upward ROE revision following strong FY25 results (please see our CRCB note here for details).

\- Rating changes: (1) We downgrade BoBJ to UW from Neutral, as we believe rising AQ risks and limited provision buffers could keep 2026E EPS growth in single digits (JPMe $5\%$ ) despite the depressed FY25 base, while its weak CET1 position may constrain loan growth and threaten dividend sustainability, implying downside risks to both EPS and DPS. Our 2026/27 profits forecasts are $-4\% / -5\%$ below Wind consensus, as we factor in higher credit cost assumptions than the Street to reflect rising risks in its loan book. (2) We downgrade BoSH to Neutral from OW, as its core earnings recovery is weaker than peers'. Meanwhile, management's strategy of stable low-single-digit EPS growth with a $c30\%$ payout ratio positioning the bank as a defensive yield name. We believe investor appetite for non-SOE bank dividend plays is fading, while regional bank investors increasingly seek higher-beta names with re-rating stories. That said, although BoSH's 2026E dividend yield of $5.5\%$ should protect downside, we see limited upside from here, given its below-peer NII/fee momentum and subdued loan growth.

Performance diverged among regional banks, and we prefer names with clearer core earnings recoveries and lower EPS downside risks. CRBs' earnings recovery in 1Q26 was driven mainly by stronger NII growth and early signs of NIM stabilization, supported by decent “good start” loan demand/pricing and deposit cost savings. Fee growth was divergent, with BoNB taking the lead. However, bottom-line profit growth was capped by higher credit costs, while capital buffers and dividend visibility became more important differentiators. Our top picks are BoNB and CRCB, while we avoid BoBJ.

list_items: - BoNB remains our top pick among regional banks, supported by the cleanest 1Q26 beat and the most visible fee upside. BoNB delivered a strong combination of core earnings recovery, fee acceleration, improving forward-looking AQ indicators and a positive dividend surprise. NII grew 14% y/y in 1Q26, supported by quality loan expansion and loan mix optimization, while fee income surged 82% y/y, significantly outperforming peers and highlighting its differentiated wealth management franchise. The bank also raised its cash dividend payout ratio to 28% in FY25 from 23% in FY24, a positive surprise to the market. Although CET1 remains a key investor concern, with the 1Q26 CET1 ratio at 9.25%, we believe BoNB's stronger earnings quality, wealth management upside and improving AQ trend should continue to support its premium valuation.

- CRCB is our preferred recovery name, as its ROE recovery remains scarce among A-share banks and is not fully reflected in valuation, in our view. CRCB's 1Q26 results showed a continued earnings recovery, with revenue and pretax profit up $8\%$ and $12\%$ y/y, respectively. We like CRCB for its improving earnings trend, relatively high capital buffer, the scarcity value of ROE recovery among A-share banks, and leverage to the growth of the Chengdu-Chongqing economic circle. The key pushback remains retail AQ, but we believe the valuation does not fully reflect the durability and quality of earnings recovery if credit costs remain manageable (please see our upgrade note here for details).

text: \- We avoid BoBJ, as rising AQ risks, limited earnings buffers and weak CET1 position imply downside risks to both EPS and DPS. BoBJ reported a 4Q25 loss due mainly to one-off impairment charges on financial investment assets, but we do not expect earnings to rebound meaningfully despite the depressed FY25 base, as loan provisioning pressure may rise alongside worsening AQ trends. The NPL ratio rose 3bps q/q in 1Q26, credit cost increased 64bps y/y, to 0.98%, and the SML/overdue loan ratios deteriorated by 11bps/43bps h/h in 2H25. BoBJ also has the lowest NPL coverage ratio among our covered regional banks, at 198% in 1Q26, limiting its ability to smooth earnings through provision release. Meanwhile, its CET1 ratio was only 8.59%, just 84bps above the regulatory minimum, which may constrain loan growth and dividend sustainability. We believe this makes BoBJ less able to participate in a potential macro recovery and leaves both EPS and DPS vulnerable to downside risks.

Downgrade BoBJ to UW from Neutral
We downgrade Bank of Beijing (BoBJ) to Underweight from Neutral with a Dec-26 PT of Rmb4.40 (16% potential downside) for the following reasons:

\- Weak earnings visibility with rising AQ risks, despite the low FY25 base. BoBJ reported a loss in 4Q25, dragged mainly by one-off impairment charges on financial investment assets, leading to a 24% y/y contraction in FY25 profits. The one-off nature suggests the sharp 4Q25 provision spike is unlikely to repeat, but such an event shows a lapse in risk management, and we do not expect a meaningful rebound in FY26 profit growth. The underlying asset quality trend continues to weaken, as indicated by the deterioration in asset quality leading indicators, such as the 12bps/43bps h/h rise in the SML ratio/overdue loan ratio at end-2025 (Figure 3), the ongoing rise in the NPL ratio (+3bps q/q) and the sharp surge in credit cost (+35bps y/y) in 1Q26 (Figure 4), dragged on mainly by consumption, mortgage and property-related loans. We expect rising loan provisioning pressure and structurally higher normalized credit costs going forward. Therefore, despite the depressed FY25 base, we expect net profit growth to be moderate in 2026, at \~5% y/y. We expect BoBJ's credit cost to rise to 99bps (+23bps y/y) in 2026, but this remains below the 116bps average during the last AQ upcycle in 2015-20, suggesting downside risks to EPS if credit costs normalize closer to historical stress-cycle levels (Figure 5). Our sensitivity analysis shows that the drag on net profit for every further 5bps increase in credit cost would be \~4.4% in 2026E (Table 4).

\- Weaker earnings buffers than at peers. BoBJ's NPL coverage ratio was $198\%$ in 1Q26, the lowest among our covered regional banks (Figure 6), indicating weaker ability to cushion earnings growth with provision release. BoBJ's OCI reserve buffer is also limited. Its OCI reserve as a $\%$ of revenue was $2\%$ in 2025 vs. peers' average of $5\%$ (Figure 7).

\- Capital constraint may limit loan expansion and weaken leverage to a macro recovery. BoBJ's CET1 ratio was only 8.59% in 1Q26, with only an 84bps buffer above the regulatory minimum requirement, the lowest among peers (Figure 2). Per the company, the bank plans to follow a “capital-constrained asset growth” approach (“以资本定资产”), suggesting loan growth is likely to remain subdued at low single digits in the absence of a clear external capital replenishment plan. 1Q26 loans grew only 1% q/q. We believe the weak capital position constrains BoBJ's future balance sheet expansion and reduces BoBJ's ability to benefit from a potential macro recovery cycle relative to peers with stronger capital flexibility.

\- Dividend yield becoming less attractive, with uncertain outlook. BoBJ raised its payout ratio to 35% in FY25 partly to stabilize shareholder return amid earnings pressure, but we do not expect such a payout level to be sustainable, given its capital constraints. Assuming the payout ratio normalizes back to \~30% (it was around 30% in 2017-24) and FY26E EPS growth recovers modestly, at \~5%, we estimate the FY26E dividend yield at \~4.8%, with downside risk if earnings or capital pressure deteriorate. In our view, the combination of reduced earnings visibility, constrained capital and lower buffer levels reduces the defensiveness of its dividend profile.

text: Downgrade BoSH to Neutral from OW
We downgrade Bank of Shanghai to Neutral from OW with a new Dec-26 PT of Rmb9.50, implying a 0.5x 2026E P/B, for the following reasons.

list_items: - Weakest core earnings trend among peers in 1Q26. BoSH's NII recovery in 1Q26 of $5\%$ y/y (vs. covered CRB peers' average of $16\%$ y/y) was the weakest among peers (Figure 8). BoSH continues to see fee contraction of $17\%$ y/y, ranking at the bottom among peers (Figure 9). Seventy-four percent of BoSH's fee income is contributed by corporate business. Thus, the bank is less leveraged to the ongoing recovery in WM business and capital-market-related fee income.

- Loan growth remains subdued, with deterioration in loan mix. Loan growth was subdued in 2025, at 2% y/y, lagging the peer average of 11% y/y and system loan growth of 6% y/y. The loan mix also deteriorated, with corporate loan growth flat y/y while lower-yield discounting bills grew 32% y/y, weighing on asset pricing. Management guided improvements in loan growth of 4% y/y in 2026, and we note marginal improvement in 1Q26, with overall loans picking up 3% q/q, though this is still below the peer average of 5% q/q (Figure 10).

- Dividend yield remains attractive, providing a defensive valuation from current levels. According to the company, BoSH aim to deliver stable low-single-digit EPS growth and maintain a payout ratio of c30% in 2026-28. We forecast its 2026 dividend yield at 5.5%, higher than at Big 4 banks (average 4.1%), making its valuation defensive from current levels (Figure 11).

Core earnings recovery: NII improved further, fee divergence widened

list_items: - Core earnings recovery continued in 1Q26, supported mainly by stronger NII growth. CRBs' average NII growth accelerated to 16% y/y in 1Q26 from 13% y/y in 4Q25, underpinned by faster loan expansion and lagged benefits from deposit cost cuts. The NII recovery was broad-based, with BoNJ, BoHZ, CRCB and BoNB reporting double-digit growth. Only three banks reported quarterly NIM, all of which show strong q/q rebounds in 1Q26. Banks generally commented that the re-pricing of high-cost time deposits continued to create room for NIM stabilization despite the sector-wide asset yield pressure. Banks guided that the magnitude of NIM contraction should narrow in 2026 vs. 2025 (-10bps on average), supporting a more resilient NII trend.

- Fee income showed clear divergence, with BoNB standing out. CRBs' average fee income grew 12% y/y in 1Q26 (vs. +9% y/y in 4Q25), but the recovery was uneven. BoNB's fee income increased 82% y/y in 1Q26, accelerating from 37% y/y in 4Q25, highlighting its differentiated wealth management franchise and its higher beta to improving capital market sentiment. By contrast, BoSH, BoNJ and BoHZ reported fee contraction of -17%/-15%/-11% y/y, suggesting that fee recovery is not yet broad-based across regional banks. CSRCB's fee income increased 41% y/y, but from a low base.

- Non-fee income remained the key drag in 1Q26, although the magnitude of contraction narrowed. CRBs' non-fee income contracted 8% y/y on average in 1Q26 vs. -32% y/y in 4Q25. The trend remained mixed by bank. BoBJ was the main positive outlier, with non-fee income up 40% y/y, helping drive its 1Q revenue recovery after the 4Q loss. In contrast, BoHZ, CRCB and BoNB all reported contractions of over 20% y/y in 1Q26. In our view, the revenue recovery is increasingly NII-led, while non-fee remains volatile and less reliable as an earnings driver.

- PPOP growth continued to recover in 1Q26, driven by stronger revenue growth and broadly disciplined opex control, although higher credit costs capped the translation into bottom-line earnings growth. CRBs' average PPOP growth accelerated to 13% y/y in 1Q26 from 3% y/y in 4Q25. Sector opex declined 3% y/y on average in 1Q26 vs. +4% y/y in 4Q25. However, stronger PPOP growth did not fully translate into earnings acceleration, as credit costs moved higher across several banks. CRBs' average net profit growth was 7% y/y in 1Q26, below the pace of PPOP growth, due mainly to rising provisioning pressure. This trend was particularly visible at BoNJ and BoBJ, where a stronger revenue recovery was partly offset by higher LLP charges and credit costs in 1Q26.

text: Steady balance sheet expansion, with corporate lending the key driver

list_items: - CRBs delivered a solid “good start” in 1Q26, with loan growth accelerating, while deposit growth remained even stronger. On average, CRBs’ loans grew 5.4% q/q in 1Q26 (vs. SOE banks’ average of +4.4% q/q), while deposits increased 7% q/q, indicating continued strong balance sheet expansion momentum.

- Corporate lending remained the main growth driver, while retail loan demand remained relatively weak. Corporate loan growth outpaced retail across regional banks in 2025, and this trend extended into 1Q26. Retail loan growth remained soft, particularly in mortgage and personal business loans. The ongoing corporate tilt in loan mix is supportive of near-term loan growth and better AQ, but may also imply lower yields and continued pressure on asset-side pricing.

- Deposit growth averaged a strong $7\%$ q/q in 1Q25 for CRBs. Solid deposit growth was due to CRB's stronger local deposit franchise in its main operating regions than at larger banks. BoNB saw the highest increase in CASA ratio (demand deposit/deposits) in 2025 (Figure 12) thanks to its comprehensive ecosystem for corporate clients, which helps retain low-cost demand deposits.

text: Asset quality: Retail risks remained the main point to watch

list_items: - Headline asset quality remained broadly stable in 1Q26, with BoBJ the laggard. CRBs' average NPL ratio remained flat q/q in 1Q26, while the average NPL coverage ratio declined 7ppts q/q, to 343%. The modest decline in coverage suggests banks are still using provision buffers to smooth earnings, although the absolute coverage level remains comfortable for most banks. BoBJ's AQ metrics were more alarming, with the 1Q26 NPL ratio up 3bps q/q and the lowest NPL coverage ratio among our covered regional banks.

- Forward-looking indicators improved q/q in 1Q26, but need to be read together with the 2H25 deterioration. For banks with disclosures, the average SML ratio declined 6bps q/q in 1Q26. BoNB was the clearest positive, with the SML ratio down 8bps q/q in 1Q26 and the NPL formation ratio down 1bp q/q. BoNJ also reported a flat q/q NPL ratio and an 11bps q/q decline in the SML ratio. However, the 2H25 semi-annual data still showed pressure in some names, especially BoBJ/CSRCB, where overdue ratios rose 43bps/29bps h/h.

- Retail asset quality remains the key pressure point, while corporate AQ improved. The average retail NPL ratio increased 7bps h/h in 2H25, while the average corporate NPL ratio declined 9bps h/h. By subsegment (Table 14-Table 15), banks in general saw higher AQ pressure from personal business. NPL ratios for mortgage loans increased 19bps h/h on average for our covered CRBs, while NPL ratios remained relatively low. CSRCB remains the name with the least clarity, given its high retail loan exposure and reduced disclosure of sector-level AQ in FY25.

text: Thin capital level becoming a bigger constraint

list_items: - Capital ratios weakened in 1Q26, and city banks in general have low CET1 capital buffers. CRBs' average CET1 ratio declined 10bps q/q in 1Q26, to 10.13%. BoBJ has the lowest capital buffer of 84bps against the minimum requirements among our covered regional banks, followed by BoNJ (142bps) and BoNB (150bps). The low capital buffer may limit room for balance sheet expansion or stable shareholder returns, especially for banks with weak profit generation.

- Dividend policies were generally supportive, but DPS outcomes differed. BoNB delivered the biggest positive surprise, raising its cash dividend payout ratio from 23% in 2024 to 28% in 2025, with the implied 2026E dividend yield at around 4.2% if bank keeps the payout ratio at 28%. BoHZ also increased its payout ratio from 24.5% to 26.4%, and CSRCB raised its cash payout ratio to 21% (+1.5 pcts y/y), while also announcing a stock dividend. By contrast, BoBJ raised its payout ratio to 35%, but DPS still declined 13% y/y due to a 28% EPS decline in 2025, bringing its 2026E dividend yield down to 4.8%.

- BoNB's capital position is becoming a key investor concern despite strong fundamentals. BoNB's CET1 ratio dropped to 9.25% in 1Q26, with a buffer of only \~150bps above the regulatory minimum, raising investor concerns about potential capital-raising, especially given its strong loan growth. As such, some investors are increasingly focused on whether BoNB may need to raise capital to sustain its above-peer loan growth trajectory. Management has indicated that capital pressure will be addressed mainly through internal accumulation and structural optimization. In particular, the bank plans to: (1) rely more on retained earnings and further develop capital-light businesses; and (2) promote migration to the IRB approach over the medium to long term to improve RWA efficiency. That said, we do not rule out the possibility of external capital-raising. Based on past capital-raising events, BoNB's share price often underperforms initially following announcement, but generally outperforms the CSI Banks Index over a one-month period thereafter (Table 17).

text: We actualize 2025 numbers and raise our FY26E/27E earnings by 0.9%/1.4%. In detail, we adjust up our fee income assumptions following the strong fee momentum in 4Q25-1Q26 and increase our NIM forecast; this is partly offset by lower non-NII and higher credit cost assumptions. We also introduce our FY28 forecast. As a result, our Dec-26 PT is revised up 1.6%, to Rmb38.80. Maintain OW.
Bank of Ningbo (Overweight; Price Target: Rmb38.80)

Bank of Ningbo differentiates itself from its small bank peers with its: (1) wealth management development strategy; (2) focus on local SME and high-net-worth retail clients; and (3) comprehensive service platforms that increase client stickiness. As a regional bank, BoNB is more flexible than larger banks to accommodate macro changes. At the same time, the bank enjoys greater economies of scale than its smaller bank peers.

BoNB's reasonable management incentive system ensures that its strategy can be effectively implemented. Meanwhile, the market-oriented mechanism suggests higher potential to expand market share and deliver growth in an upward market cycle.

We think BoNB can maintain better ROE than its peers, aided by: (1) its attractive risk-adjusted asset yield and strong funding franchise; (2) its prudent risk management, especially in higher-risk sectors; (3) its development of capital-light business, i.e., fee business; and (4) the strength of Ningbo's local economy.
Our Dec-26 PT of Rmb38.80 is based on a DDM, assuming a cost of capital of 13.9%, a normalized ROE of 13.5% and a terminal date of 31 December 2028.
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Downside risks include lower-than-expected fee growth, higher-than-expected NIM contraction, and a deterioration in SME asset quality.
Upside catalysts include NIM expansion, higher-than-expected loan and fee growth, and better-than-expected macro growth.

- Management guided to stable EPS growth in 2026. We believe provision and cost management could cushion earnings growth if there is downside risk to revenues. However, lackluster long-term risk-adjusted returns and a weak franchise will likely lead to soft profitability momentum.

Jiangsu Changshu Rural Commercial Bank Limited

list_items: - CSRCB has developed its own small business loan model to capture the niche individual business loan market, allowing it to avoid direct competition with larger banks in the local area. This strategy has helped it to achieve the highest retail loan yield among the CRBs we cover with a relatively stable asset quality.

- CSRCB has a nationwide village bank license available for wide expansion. This expansion potential is rare, given the generally unconstructive regulatory approach to CRBs expanding in different areas. Meanwhile, CSRCB is able to replicate its successful experience in Changshu quickly to new branches, as it puts the risk control and loan approval functions in its back office.

- Rising asset quality risks from the retail side are a major concern. As the SME economy remains weak, we note upticks in the forward-looking AQ indicators (SML % and overdue %) and NPL formation. In addition, fierce competition and weak demand have pushed the bank to increase its exposure to credit loans, which are subject to higher risks.
